articles.title: Takeaways from Mullin's House testimony on cyber outages, the Texas-LSU flight and immigration
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, t...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin , in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country's immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

"I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions," Clayton said. "But based on what we know today," he said, "these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack."

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services ; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation's air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps ; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry ; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

"I'm 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems," Mullin said.

Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin's Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump's original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights .

Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

"If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly," Mullin said.

Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.

Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration's telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the public clear answers.

"We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn't have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring surge, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The employment rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.

Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.

The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump's immigration agenda.

Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.

"You are killing people," McIver replied.

"No ma'am. That's your opinion," Mullin said, ending the exchange.

Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.

Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff .

Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

articles.title: US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says in visit to Caracas
articles.summary: CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties that will range from conducting joint training to i...
articles.body:
CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties that will range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday in Caracas while visiting the South American nation's interim leaders.

Hegseth touted how U.S. forces in January captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro , telling an audience of diplomats and military officials from both countries that now Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."

He also praised the "close cooperation" with acting President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials "to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all," in a reference to drug traffickers.

Hegseth's visit, the latest in a series of stops in Venezuela by members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet, underscores efforts by the U.S. administration to deepen its influence in the South American country. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves .

Hegseth praises Trump's Venezuela oil deal

The Pentagon chief praised the energy deal by referencing another major military action by the Trump administration this year — the Iran war . The conflict has disrupted global energy supplies through a critical waterway in the Persian Gulf, raising gasoline prices and contributing to the Republican Party's severe losses in this month's midterm elections.

The Venezuela oil deal "makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere," Hegseth said at the U.S. Embassy in Caracas.

In the meeting with Hegseth, Rodríguez asserted that the deal enables "the energy development of our nations" and "benefits both the people of the United States and the people of Venezuela."

Among those in attendance for Hegseth's speech was Alejandro Betancourt, the owner of North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest oil operator in Venezuela. The U.S. government and Betancourt's company entered into the ambitious agreement to tap Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Both the Interior and Energy secretaries also visited Venezuela earlier this year and focused their efforts on tapping its oil reserves and critical minerals . The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.

Hegseth later stopped in Bogota, Colombia, where he was greeted at a military base by the country's defense and foreign ministers.

Few details provided on the US-Venezuela military agreement

Hegseth offered few specifics on what the military agreement would entail, beyond saying that the two countries' militaries would be "training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence, more defense equipment and capabilities together."

Speaking separately, Rodríguez said she hoped the countries' military cooperation "can be brought to its highest possible level" to allow them to "address common threats."

Hegseth pointed to Venezuela partnering with the U.S. "to recover its territory from narco-terrorist networks." The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

The development comes as the U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump's return to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.

To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls "narco-terrorists" in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs or that they have made an impact on the availability of drugs in the country.

Hegseth also used his speech to boast about the military operation that seized Maduro, calling it "the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America" that "lasted just 48 minutes."

"America's best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours," he added.

But Venezuela's ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.

Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader "predicted," the operation ended with "no war, yes, peace."

Uncertainty about Venezuela's political future

Hegseth's visit also comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.

Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro's capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela's head of state.

Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for "working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela."

Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the "safe" return of the politician was the result of "reconciliation talks" supported by the U.S., which he considered "the best opportunity" Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.

The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House's decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela's oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.

Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: A TV host announced she's pregnant at 59. How motherhood is changing
articles.summary: A TV host stunned her co-hosts when she announced she's pregnant at 59. She's part of a growing trend of women having children later in life.
articles.body:
A British news show host announced she's pregnant at age 59, leaving her co-hosts speechless on live television.

Dr. Renée Hoenderkamp, a GB News co-host and National Health Service general practitioner, revealed during a Nov. 14 broadcast that she's 12 weeks pregnant with her third child, nearly four decades after the birth of her first.

"I'm a mother of a grown-up boy and a very young girl. And I have some news to break to the panel today that they're not aware of or anybody else for that matter: I'm actually going to be a mother of three shortly," Hoenderkamp said during the show.

Hoenderkamp is mom to 37-year-old Calum and an 8-year-old Alice.

While the news clearly stunned her co-hosts and many who saw the news online responded with similar levels of surprise, in recent years, research shows that more and more women are having kids into their 40s and 50s.

For example, in the United States, while birth rates are down , fertility rates have risen among women 40 and older. From 2023 to 2024, birth rates declined for women aged 15-34, stayed unchanged for women aged 35-39 and rose 2% for women aged 40-44, according to data released in July of 2025.

Famous faces like Anne Hathaway , 44, and Hilary Swank , 52, have also made headlines in recent months for their pregnancies. Swank who is expecting her third child, addressed shock over her pregnancy during a Nov. 17 appearance on U.K. show "This Morning ": "It's time to get with the times! We're so advanced in our world, people are living so much longer, you know, and so many women are wanting to wait until later. It's becoming quite a normal thing to have children later."

Later in the broadcast, Hoenderkamp explained that she had frozen eggs in her 30s and traveled to Poland to have the eggs implanted through in vitro fertilization.

Since her announcement, Hoenderkamp hit back on comments calling her selfish, sharing that she feels more prepared to be a mother now than in her youth.

"Now I am back (online), for all of the thousands of messages congratulating me on the news of my new daughter - THANK YOU!!!! For the rest - I don't care what you think," she wrote in a Nov. 15 post on X .

She spoke out further in essays she penned for the Daily Mail and GB News on Nov. 17, in which she shared that she had her first child when she was 21 and her second child at 51.

She wrote, "I know I have been a better mother in my fifties than when I was 21," explaining that "age, wisdom, patience and financial stability do make for better parenting."

Hoenderkamp wrote that the reaction to the news has been "interesting."

"Alongside the kind messages there have been words like 'disgusting,' 'revolting,' 'selfish' and 'wrong,'" Hoenderkamp said. "The objection appears to rest on a number on a birth certificate."

She pointed out that the baby's father is now 66, but "almost no one" has commented on his age.

"He has been able, because of the stage of life he is in, to be a present father rather than the man who brings home the money and is rarely seen," Hoenderkamp wrote. "Society rarely objects when men become fathers at 70 or 80. The double standard is hard to miss."

What to know about later-in-life pregnancies

Family planning is personal, and there are myriad reasons why more women are waiting to have kids, Dr. Lora Shahine , a reproductive endocrinologist at Ivy Fertility's Pacific Northwest Fertility clinic in Seattle, previously told USA TODAY. A 2022 survey from the Institute for Family Studies found that among women aged 18-55 who want more children, 44% cited not finding the right partner as a barrier, 36% cited affordability and 25% cited lifestyle or career.

Factors like affordability and lack of familial support can impact that decision.

Shahine said she sees a lot of women who are trying to plan their pregnancies several years, or even a decade, in advance and making "really thoughtful decisions about when and how they build their family." Some of them are scared about the health risks involved in older pregnancies.

While it's routine and possible for women to have children in their 40s, Shahine said age does impact fertility and how long it might take to get pregnant, including the risk of miscarriage.

"I think there's a common assumption that fertility treatment can overcome anything," Shahine said.

And women who become pregnant later in life face increased risks of gestational diabetes and preeclampsia, as well as complications that require cesarean delivery, according to John Hopkins Medicine . The risk of miscarriage, frequently due to fetal chromosomal abnormalities, also increases with age, as do preterm birth and stillbirth.

Egg freezing and in-vitro fertilization are important tools to help with fertility struggles in older mothers, Danielle Melfi, CEO of Resolve , a fertility patient advocacy group, previously told USA TODAY. More women are choosing to freeze their eggs than ever before, she said.

"While egg freezing isn't a guarantee," Melfi said, "it does help women feel like they have more time to make some of these decisions."

Everyone is different, Shahine said, and women shouldn't make assumptions about their fertility based on the women in their family who have become mothers before them.

"Our biggest piece of advice is consulting with your doctor," Melfi said.

articles.title: Four days after a deadly Brooklyn building collapse forced her family to evacuate, 13-year-old Zariah Coleman got her missing cat Isaac back after rescuers heard a faint meow coming from a kitchen cabinet
articles.summary: A 13-year-old girl in Brooklyn has been reunited with her missing cat after four days of uncertainty following a deadly building collapse that forced her
articles.body: A 13-year-old girl in Brooklyn has been reunited with her missing cat after four days of uncertainty following a deadly building collapse that forced her family to leave their home. Isaac was found alive inside a kitchen cabinet beneath the sink, where he had been hiding since the disaster. The rescue involved New York City’s Department of Buildings, the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare and animal welfare nonprofit Flatbush Cats. The Associated Press, Gothamist and ABC7 New York reported on the discovery, which brought a moment of relief to a family affected by the tragedy. The collapse occurred on Wednesday, November 11, in the Flatbush neighbourhood of Brooklyn, killing eight people and injuring 18 others. The incident also damaged neighbouring buildings, forcing residents to evacuate as emergency services secured the area. Among those displaced were Zariah Coleman and her mother, whose apartment was left exposed after the collapse tore away part of the adjoining structure, leaving a hole where the teenager’s bedroom wall had been.For Zariah, the immediate worry was finding Isaac, who had been inside the apartment when the disaster occurred. Unable to return home because of safety restrictions, the family had no way of knowing whether their pet had survived or where he might be hiding. The teenager’s emotional appeal for help came during a news conference on Friday, November 13. She explained that she feared Isaac was frightened and hiding somewhere inside the apartment. Her plea attracted widespread attention, with footage of her speaking about the missing cat circulating online.Among those who saw the appeal was Will Zweigart, executive director of Flatbush Cats, a Brooklyn-based animal rescue organisation. He decided to help locate Isaac but soon discovered that entering the property would require coordination with several city agencies. The area remained restricted because of structural safety concerns and the ongoing investigation into the collapse.According to Gothamist, Zweigart spent two days working with officials, including Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, to obtain permission to enter the apartment. The Department of Buildings eventually approved the search for Sunday, November 15. Zweigart entered the property alongside Yegal Shamash, the Department of Buildings’ first deputy commissioner. Carrying rescue equipment, a pet carrier and food to attract the cat, the team carefully searched the damaged apartment.The initial search proved unsuccessful. Rescuers checked several rooms, closets and potential hiding places but could not find Isaac. During a final sweep of the kitchen, however, Zweigart heard a faint meow coming from a cabinet beneath the sink.When he checked, he discovered the frightened cat hiding among the items stored inside. The team initially attempted to lure Isaac into an open carrier using food, but he remained reluctant to come out. After carefully clearing the cabinet and making space for him, the rescuers managed to coax him into the carrier.Isaac had survived four days without food or water. Despite the ordeal, he appeared to be in reasonably good condition, although he was hungry and vocal. He was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for an examination and further care. Outside the building, Zariah and her mother had been waiting anxiously for news. When the rescuers emerged with Isaac, the teenager was finally able to see her pet again. She greeted him while he remained inside his carrier, bringing an emotional end to the search.The rescue was particularly significant because Isaac is an approved emotional support animal for Zariah. Taylor highlighted the importance of returning the cat to the family, who had already experienced considerable trauma following the collapse. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani also acknowledged the efforts of the teams involved, thanking the Department of Buildings, the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare and Flatbush Cats for helping locate Isaac and reunite him with his owner.Although the family was able to see Isaac immediately after the rescue, he remained under veterinary observation. Officials said he would be formally reunited with Zariah at Flatbush Veterinary Clinic on Monday, November 16. For a family dealing with displacement and the aftermath of a devastating incident, the recovery of their pet offered a rare moment of happiness. After four days of uncertainty, Zariah finally had the reassurance that Isaac had survived and would soon be home with her again.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Texas homeowners challenged an 88-acre data centre planned close to their houses, fearing noise and environmental effects; a settlement offers nearly $1.9 million and protections but allows the project
articles.summary: Texas homeowners near Westlake challenged an 88 acre data centre planned close to their houses, fearing noise, drainage problems, and environmental
articles.body: Texas homeowners near Westlake challenged an 88 acre data centre planned close to their houses, fearing noise, drainage problems, and environmental effects. A settlement between developer PowerHouse, the City of Keller, and affected residents offers nearly $1.9 million and new protections, but it allows the project to move forward, according to NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth and the Town of Westlake.The facility, planned near the northeast corner of U.S. 377 and Westport Parkway, would include four buildings totaling about 1.1 million square feet. The site sits roughly 500 feet from some residents’ backyards, which is why the project became a flashpoint for the Lakes of Marshall Ridge neighbourhood.Why residents pushed backResidents in Keller’s Marshall Ridge area worried that the data centre would bring noise, traffic, and environmental disruption too close to their homes. Their concerns were strong enough to become the basis of a lawsuit challenging the project.The proposed site is in Westlake’s commercial and industrial area, but its proximity to residential backyards made the issue personal. For people living nearby, the question was not whether data centres are useful, but whether one could operate responsibly at that distance.The dispute also reflected a broader tension between economic development and quality of life. Westlake leaders saw the project as a major revenue opportunity, while residents saw a risk to their neighbourhood.What the settlement providesThe settlement, signed on November 5, requires PowerHouse to pay nearly $1.9 million within 45 days. The payment includes $1.5 million for a noise mitigation fund, $300,000 for fire protection, and $76,000 to cover Keller’s legal and consulting costs.The agreement also sets specific limits on how the facility can operate. Noise is capped at 49 decibels overnight between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., and 56 decibels during the day, measured at residential property lines, as per the report.Other protections include a taller berm, longer sound monitoring, and restrictions on diesel generator testing. The settlement also moves construction staging farther away from homes.How the project will be managedThe developer must increase the proposed berm from 8 feet to 10 feet. Sound monitoring is extended from one year to three years, giving residents a longer window to see whether the limits are being met.More than half of the trees in the buffer must be evergreens, with replacements required for trees that die. Diesel backup generators must meet EPA Tier 4 emissions standards, and testing is restricted to between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.These requirements are meant to reduce the impact on nearby residents. They do not eliminate the project, but they create a framework for how it must operate.What Westlake gainsWestlake Mayor Kim Greaves said the data centre would generate about $5 million a year for the town over its first 10 years. That would increase the town’s revenue by about 14 percent, according to NBC 5.The Town of Westlake says the project is expected to generate roughly $5 million annually for the first decade and about $7 million annually thereafter. The town describes this as a long term source of revenue for services, infrastructure, and future priorities.The settlement also makes clear that Westlake taxpayers will not pay for the agreement. All settlement related obligations are covered by PowerHouse, and the town’s attorney fees were fully reimbursed.Why the project still divides peopleEven after the settlement, the project continues to draw mixed reactions. During public comment, some residents expressed frustration with the town’s handling of the development, while others argued that data centres are an important part of growing infrastructure.One resident said the town had never wanted people to know the truth about what was going on. Another described the project as irresponsible, calling it a big stinking pile of BS.Supporters took a different view. They argued that communities, counties, and states cannot fear information processing infrastructure, and that power and water concerns are solvable.What happens nextWith the settlement in place, the project has a clear path forward. The Westlake Town Council approved the development agreement on November 12, clearing another hurdle after months of legal disputes and public pushback.The agreement does not erase the concerns of nearby residents. It does, however, give them specific protections and a financial commitment from the developer.For Westlake, the project represents a major economic opportunity. For the residents closest to the site, it represents a compromise that allows the data centre to proceed while trying to limit its impact.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Canadian son believed family company shares entitled him to property assets, but his father's estate plans favoured his sister; a judge rejected his claim while ordering the companies to release financial records
articles.summary: A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has dismissed a son's legal challenge against his family's property companies, finding that he failed to prove
articles.body: A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has dismissed a son's legal challenge against his family's property companies, finding that he failed to prove "oppressive conduct" despite believing that his company shares gave him rights to specific family assets. The case was heard in Vancouver and involved a dispute between the applicant, described in the court records as "the Petitioner", and several family-owned companies and other respondents, including his father and sister. The son argued that being a shareholder in the family companies meant he was entitled to own certain properties held by those businesses.The Petitioner asked the court to intervene, claiming that the companies and other respondents had engaged in "oppressive or unfairly prejudicial conduct". His main complaint was that his father's plans for distributing his estate were unfair and favoured his sister over him. He believed these decisions went against his expectations as a shareholder. However, Madam Justice J.G. Harris rejected his understanding of shareholder rights. In written reasons delivered on November 17, 2026, Justice Harris said the son's complaints were mainly about inheritance and family arrangements, rather than corporate oppression.Understanding shareholder rightsThe judge explained a basic rule of company law: shareholders own shares in a company, not the individual properties or other assets that the company owns. Justice Harris said the "Petitioner's view that he is entitled to the assets of the numbered companies by virtue of his status as a shareholder is legally misconceived." The court found that the son's disagreement with his father's estate plans and the way the family companies managed their assets did not amount to oppression under the province's Business Corporations Act.Justice Harris ruled that the son had "failed to establish that the respondents engaged in conduct that was oppressive, unfairly prejudicial, or that unfairly disregarded his interests as a shareholder." The judge also explained that disputes over the father's estate and alleged promises about how assets would be distributed in the future were separate legal matters. They could not be dealt with through a corporate oppression claim. In other words, the fact that the son held shares in the family companies did not automatically give him ownership of the properties registered in their names. His rights as a shareholder were linked to his investment in the businesses, not to direct control over their individual assets.Family estate planning disagreementsAlthough the court rejected the main oppression claim, the respondents did not win on every issue. The Petitioner had also asked for access to the financial and corporate records of the family businesses. He said he needed the documents to understand how the companies operated and to assess the value of his shares. The respondents opposed the request. They argued that the son's main legal claim had no merit and that giving him access to the records could create an unnecessary burden or allow the information to be used improperly.Madam Justice Harris disagreed with the companies on this point and granted the request for access to relevant corporate and financial information. The judge explained that shareholders have a basic right to inspect company records, subject to certain conditions. That right does not automatically disappear because a shareholder has brought other legal claims that may fail or be disputed. The order therefore allowed the son to obtain relevant information about the family companies, even though his broader allegation of corporate oppression had been dismissed.The ruling draws a distinction between disputes over inheritance and the legal rights that come with owning company shares. A disagreement with a parent's estate plans, including claims that one child has been favoured over another, does not by itself establish that a company has treated a shareholder unfairly. The court's decision confirms that shareholders have rights in the companies in which they invest, but those rights do not make them the direct owners of corporate property. The son's request for company records was granted, while his attempt to use corporate oppression law to challenge his father's estate planning decisions was rejected.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bombay HC nixes nod to prosecute ex-ICICI Bank chief Kochhar
articles.summary: Bombay High Court quashes ICICI Bank’s sanction to prosecute ex-CEO Chanda Kochhar, halting CBI’s Prevention of Corruption Act bribery case in Videocon loans probe.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Holding that it was illegal, Bombay HC on Wednesday quashed and set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank in 2023 to prosecute its former MD and CEO, Chanda Kochhar, over alleged irregularities in loans provided to Venugopal Dhoot-led Videocon Group between 2009 and 2011. It said the authority that gave the nod “completely failed to apply its mind” and the competent authority in this case—RBI—had passed no such sanction order.It set aside the consequential actions taken by the special court in the CBI case pursuant to the sanction order.The HC order means CBI cannot proceed against Kochhar under Prevention of Corruption Act and its case against her falls. The agency can appeal the ruling.Justice Milind Jadhav said the “power of removal vests with RBI and RBI only”. “No reasons are given by RBI for removal of the petitioner (Kochhar)... Reasons for removal/sanction order are not recorded in writing by RBI,” HC said.It noted that nullity of sanction goes to the “root of the prosecution’s case” and stands on the “same pedestal as absent sanction”.Kochhar had petitioned HC in 2024 to challenge as illegal the sanction granted by ICICI Bank’s board of directors to prosecute her. Senior counsel Aabad Ponda, representing her, argued that prior sanction is necessary for any prosecution of a public servant under Prevention of Corruption Act’s Section 19, which had been invoked against her. A bank employee is considered a public servant. Ponda said the sanction was illegal as it failed to even specify the offences for which it is granted, as mandatory under the law. Besides, he said, the bank’s board of directors was not the “competent authority” to grant the sanction under the Act.HC agreed. It said the sanction was granted by an “incompetent authority”, rendering it “illegal and a nullity”.It said even the “cognisance taken by the special court of the offence under the Act is illegal and deserves to be set aside”. “Though it is true that the trial has not commenced, the very fact that cognisance is taken on the basis of the impugned defective sanction itself nullifies all past and future procedure followed by the special court,” HC said.Ponda argued that law empowered RBI to remove a chairperson, director, chief executive officer or other officer or employee of a banking company and, therefore, it was the competent authority to remove Kochhar, and not the bank’s board of directors. HC concurred.Additional solicitor general Anil Singh for CBI argued that Kochhar herself had said the bank’s board was the competent authority and stood precluded from now arguing that it was not. “I cannot countenance” it, as such a submission cannot be used to bypass legal provisions, said Justice Jadhav. Besides, the law mandates a “reasonable opportunity” for a representation to RBI when removing such high-ranking officers, HC noted.Only a letter addressed by CBI and its report, not the material collected by the agency, were placed before the bank’s board of directors to decide on the sanction, HC observed.HC said the sanction order was “unsustainable in law, being a nullity” and deserved to be quashed and set aside. It declined a request by CBI lawyer Kuldeep Patil to stay its judgment for eight weeks to enable the agency to go in for an appeal.CBI had lodged an FIR in 2019 under Indian Penal Code and Prevention of Corruption Act against Kochhar, husband Deepak, Dhoot, Nupower Renewables and Videocon Industries for allegedly defrauding ICICI Bank of Rs 1,730 crore till March 2012. Kochhar was prosecuted for conspiring with other co-accused in sanctioning a term loan of Rs 300 crore to Videocon Group. CBI arrested her and her husband, Deepak Kochhar, on Dec 23, 2022. HC granted them interim bail on Jan 9, 2023, observing that the arrest memos appeared “casual, mechanical and perfunctory, clearly without application of mind.” In June that year, CBI told the special court that ICICI Bank’s board had granted prosecution sanction against Kochhar on April 22, citing an apparent quid pro quo.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Meet Anne Liang, the 19-year-old Montreal student who organised a thrift fashion show with 30 student models, reached 68,000 people on Instagram and inspired Dawson College to make it an annual event
articles.summary: Anne Liang, a 19-year-old student at Dawson College in Montreal, organised a thrift fashion show to encourage people to enjoy fashion without supporting
articles.body: Anne Liang, a 19-year-old student at Dawson College in Montreal, organised a thrift fashion show to encourage people to enjoy fashion without supporting fast fashion. The ‘Thrifted Runway’ event featured 30 student models wearing high-fashion thrifted looks and wearable art. In an interview with Canada's National Observer, Anne Liang said more than 100 students and faculty attended or helped with the show as models, moderators, and volunteers. The event also reached 48,000 people through its Instagram feed and another 20,000 through Liang’s personal account. The college plans to make the show an annual tradition. Liang hopes to take the idea beyond campus and curate a thrift fashion show for people across Montreal.How did Anne Liang turn the ‘Thrifted Runway’ show into a runway successLiang conceived and organised the ‘Thrifted Runway’ show as a way to challenge the fast fashion industry. 30 students modelled favourite high-fashion thrifted looks and wearable art. More than 100 students and faculty attended or contributed as models, moderators and volunteers. Some participants wore clothes they had already bought second-hand. Others worked with local thrift store Spice Daddy to put together outfits they liked.The event also included a student marketplace, where people sold lightly worn clothing and kept all the money they made. The show reached 48,000 people through its Instagram feed, while Liang’s personal account reached another 20,000. Its success led the college to plan an annual event for students across the Dawson College campus.Anne Liang promotes affordable fashion and textbook reuse at Dawson CollegeLiang said she wanted people who enjoy fashion to see that personal style does not have to mean spending a fortune or harming people and the planet. According to Liang, Montreal sees itself as Canada’s fashion capital, and she hopes to organise a thrift fashion show for the wider city. The project’s runway coordinator, Myrica-Gale Monateri-Kubeck, shares that vision, and the two plan to develop the idea together as a team.Liang also worked to maintain a book exchange service at Dawson College. It helps students buy textbooks more cheaply while keeping usable materials out of landfill. The service expanded to include supplies. Science students can borrow lab coats left by graduates rather than buy a new $40 coat if they forget theirs.Anne Liang used her student union role to turn sustainability into actionThe book exchange was part of Liang’s wider work on practical sustainability. Alongside textbooks and borrowed lab coats, the service gives away notebooks and pencil cases left in lockers at the end of each term. Liang said many students struggle financially, making this support important.In an interview with Canada's National Observer, Liang shared her successful experience:“I ran for Dawson Student Union vice president of sustainability, promising to show sustainability can be a benefit, not a burden, with high-fashion thrifting as one example. Fashion is catchy. I got elected. This was my first experience organizing a major event. I started by meeting students who were interested, then we built support within the student body and other groups. The Dawson’s Campus Life department was very supportive. Dawson College was very supportive. It is true that many hands made light work.”Young people urged to turn environmental concerns into meaningful actionLiang encouraged young people not to let social media take away their hope, but to join groups and act with others. She also asked older readers to support and actively involve young people, with some students focused on modelling careers being reluctant to acknowledge the harms built into the fashion industry.She said, “There are days I feel anxious. Social media shows landfills full of discarded clothes one moment, then urges you to buy fast fashion the next. It can create the feeling that everyone else is consuming, and you are the only one worried about waste. That can be scary. But Dawson College has helped me remember that when we feel overwhelmed, we can cope best in a community of others taking action together.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Sydney homeowner hired his wife's uncle to build two houses for nearly $1.5 million, but a court found 127 defects and ordered the builder to pay $346,580
articles.summary: A Sydney homeowner who hired a relative to construct two houses for almost $1.5 million has won a substantial legal battle after a court found serious
articles.body: A Sydney homeowner who hired a relative to construct two houses for almost $1.5 million has won a substantial legal battle after a court found serious problems with the building work. The dispute involved Elrob Construction Group and homeowner Sami Haddad, whose builder was also his wife's uncle. After examining the construction contracts, expert reports and claims from both sides, the New South Wales District Court ruled in Haddad's favour, ordering the building company to pay more than $346,000 in compensation and other amounts.Court orders builder to pay around $346,000 over defects in two Sydney housesThe New South Wales District Court in Elrob Construction Group Pty Ltd v Haddad handed down its decision on 24 September 2025. The ruling said the dispute was over two double-storey brick houses with flat roofs built on land at Sans Souci in Sydney.In 2017, homeowner Sami Haddad signed two building contracts with Elrob Construction Group. The initial value of each contract was $678,220 (excluding GST) for a combined total of $1,492,084 (including GST).Elia Elrob Boujaoude, the company's principal, was responsible for the building work. He was also Haddad's wife's uncle, making the dispute particularly complicated because of the family connection.The contracts covered the construction of two separate houses, identified as 55 and 55A. The land was intended to be subdivided so that each property would have its own allotment. Haddad planned to live in one of the houses.According to the judgment, construction began around August 2018, and Boujaoude said the work had been completed by early November 2019.How did the building dispute between the relatives beginThe relationship between Haddad and Boujaoude became strained after problems emerged with the construction. In August 2020, Haddad lodged a complaint with NSW Fair Trading, alleging that the houses contained defective and unfinished work.The situation had already attracted attention from the building certifier. On 18 September 2020, the certifier issued a list of outstanding work that needed to be completed before an occupation certificate could be issued. This meant the properties had not met all the requirements for formal approval for occupation.A rectification order was subsequently issued against Elrob Construction Group on 15 December 2020, requiring attention to the defective and incomplete work.The ‘news,’ which covered the court dispute, described the condition of the properties as particularly poor. Problems reportedly included improperly installed pipes, cracked brickwork, inadequate painting, unfinished kitchens and bathrooms, exposed electrical wiring and missing flooring. Building debris and other unfinished work also contributed to the condition of the houses.The defects were not limited to cosmetic issues. Some concerned the way essential parts of the properties had been installed or finished, raising concerns about their suitability for occupation.What problems did the court identify in the propertiesThe court examined evidence from two building consultants, Anthony Capaldi and Mario Bournelis, who prepared reports and participated in a joint assessment of the disputed work.Their findings included cracks in rendered walls, poorly finished concrete, incorrectly installed drainage pipes and missing expansion joints in the brickwork.Some defects were relatively minor finishing issues, while others required more significant repair work. For example, experts identified issues with bathroom tiles where uneven grout lines resulted in finished surfaces that didn’t look consistent. The court also found insufficient waterproofing in wet areas and drainage problems that could allow water to intrude into parts of the buildings.In one case, the court considered the installation of downpipes that were not properly connected to the stormwater system. This arrangement meant that the homeowner had to monitor the rainwater tank and occasionally change pipe connections to prevent it from overflowing.The ruling also dealt with absent weep holes, which help manage moisture in masonry walls, and cracks occurring because no proper expansion joints were put in. These joints are important because if there is not enough space for movement the brickwork can expand and crack.The “news” report said that 127 defects and incomplete items were found at the two properties, indicating the extent of the construction problems.The builder's payment claim was rejectedElrob Construction Group also attempted to recover additional payments from Haddad, arguing that it was owed money for changes made during the building process.The company submitted claims for variations, including additional work associated with the properties. It sought $89,958.15, including GST, for variations relating to one of the houses. It also made an alternative claim for payment based on the value of the work it said had benefited the homeowner.However, the court was not satisfied that the builder had established its entitlement to the additional amount. The court ultimately threw out Elrob’s claim and ruled for Haddad on the cross-claim of the homeowner.The judgment found the builder liable for defective and incomplete work that was in breach of the construction contracts and the applicable statutory warranties.How much was the builder ordered to payOn 24 September 2025, District Court Judge Susanne Cole ordered Elrob Construction Group to pay Haddad a total of $346,580.91 through three separate amounts.The largest portion was $226,446.39 in damages for defective and incomplete building work. The builder was also ordered to pay $25,000 in liquidated damages under the contracts because of delays in achieving practical completion.A further $95,134.52 was awarded as restitution. This related to money Haddad had previously paid following an earlier payment adjudication under the Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment Act.Together, these amounts brought the court-ordered payment to $346,580.91. The decision also meant that Elrob's attempt to recover additional variation payments was unsuccessful.According to the NSW Government's Building Commission, the Home Building Act 1989 provides statutory warranties covering residential building work. Homeowners generally have 6 years to commence proceedings for major defects and 2 years for other defects. These periods run from the completion of the building work, subject to additional provisions in certain circumstances.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Noah Wyle, named Sexiest Man Alive, teams up with FIGS to donate $2 million towards erasing $200 million in medical debt for over 150,000 Americans; says medical debt devastates families
articles.summary: Actor Noah Wyle, who recently earned the title of PEOPLE's Sexiest Man Alive, is using his influence to support a major charitable initiative.
articles.body: Actor Noah Wyle, who recently earned the title of PEOPLE's Sexiest Man Alive, is using his influence to support a major charitable initiative. The The Pitt star has teamed up with healthcare apparel company FIGS to help more than 150,000 Americans get relief from at least $200 million in medical debt.Announcing the initiative on Tuesday, November 17, FIGS revealed that both Wyle and the company would contribute $1 million each towards the effort. The initiative is being carried out in partnership with Undue Medical Debt, a non-profit organisation that works to eliminate medical debt for financially vulnerable individuals and families across the United States.According to the announcement, every $1 donated permanently erases at least $100 in qualifying medical debt for some of the most burdened individuals and families in the country.Noah Wyle opens up about the impact of medical debtSpeaking about the initiative, Wyle highlighted how medical debt can affect families long after they have received treatment.“Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation and changes the whole experience of care,” the actor said in a statement.He added, “I'm grateful to be part of something that's taking real pressure off families and the extraordinary people trying to help them.”Wyle serves as Global FIGS Ambassador and executive producer. Through the partnership, he is lending his support to an initiative that aims to ease the financial burden of medical expenses for thousands of American households.Noah Wyle on being named PEOPLE's Sexiest Man AliveThe charitable announcement comes weeks after Wyle was named PEOPLE's Sexiest Man Alive on October 27. The actor previously revealed that his wife, Sara, encouraged him to accept the honour, although he initially found the idea difficult to believe.“I thought that sounded like a prank,” he recalled.“Just not in a million years did I think that this would be an honor bestowed on me,” he added.Wyle credited his wife for convincing him to embrace the recognition, saying she felt it reflected positively on her choice of partner.“She's the reason I accepted because she was very pleased that this reflects well on her taste. She thinks I'm a good guy and that the kind of person that I am and the kind of father I am, the kind of husband I am, is worth promoting. I thought, 'Okay, if you say so,'” he said.How Noah Wyle's family reacted to his Sexiest Man Alive titleWyle also shared how his family reacted to his new title. While Sara was amused by seeing her husband on the magazine cover, his older children had particularly memorable responses.The actor shares an 11-year-old daughter, Frances, with Sara. He is also father to son Owen, 24, and daughter Auden, 21, from his previous marriage to Tracy Warbin.Recalling his children's reactions, Wyle said his son was more concerned about the attention that would come with the recognition.“My son is super practical. He was like, 'Oh, this is going to make my life so much harder now. But that's cool, Dad. But also, you invite a lot of haters too.'”His older daughter, meanwhile, was surprised by the announcement. “My older daughter was just like, 'No way, no way.' Because I think she's going to tease me about this for the next 50 years,” he said, laughing.As for whether the title would change his life, Wyle responded with humour, joking that he hoped everything would be “wine and roses, milk and honey” from then on. However, he admitted that he expected plenty of teasing from friends and family.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A New Jersey family lost their 8-year-old daughter to an aggressive brain tumour and founded a nonprofit in her memory; it now sends care packages to children with cancer across the US
articles.summary: Olivia Grace Lipnicky lost her life to a tumour on November 6, 2019, after months of treatment and a battle with an aggressive form of cancer.
articles.body: Olivia Grace Lipnicky lost her life to a tumour on November 6, 2019, after months of treatment and a battle with an aggressive form of cancer. During her illness, Olivia remained concerned about other children facing cancer and even raised more than $10,000 for paediatric cancer research. After her death, her family carried forward her compassion by creating the ‘Liv Like a Unicorn’ Foundation.A friend's small weekly surprise during Olivia's chemotherapy had once given her something to smile about before hospital visits. According to Liv Like a Unicorn, its Unicorn Club now provides year-round support to children with cancer across the United States. The nonprofit also offers financial assistance to eligible families in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania to help cover essential household expenses during a child's treatment.How did Olivia’s fight against cancer lead to the creation of a foundationOlivia was seven when she began complaining of shoulder pain, a few weeks before her eighth birthday. Her family initially thought it was linked to a snowboarding fall. After the pain worsened and she began waking at night, they sought further medical help.An MRI at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia revealed a tumour in her spinal cord. Surgery lasted 14 hours, but doctors could remove only 40% of the tumour. Olivia came out of the operation unable to walk or use her right arm. On March 1, the family learned that the tumour was a diffuse midline glioma with the H3 K27M mutation. Because of this mutation, doctors upgraded her cancer to stage 4 and said it was similar to DIPG. Life changed overnight. The family was told she had an estimated 6 to 9 months to live and encouraged to spend the time making memories together. That is when their real fight began.Olivia raised $10,000 for cancer research before her condition worsenedAfter 6 weeks of radiation, Olivia joined a clinical trial for a medication called Onc201. For a time, she regained most of her abilities, had no symptoms, and enjoyed the summer. She also worried about other children with cancer and organised a fundraiser for paediatric cancer research. That summer, she raised more than $10,000. Her family began preparing for her return to school, but severe headaches brought her back to hospital.Doctors found that the cancer had spread to several places, including her spine, spinal fluid and the ventricles of her brain. Olivia was taken by ambulance to her treating hospital, NYU, on October 6, 2019. Their little girl passed away in her mother's arms on November 6, 2019.How a small act of kindness inspired the Unicorn ClubThe idea for the Unicorn Club came from a difficult part of Olivia’s treatment. Chemotherapy took place every Thursday, and the medication arrived in a hazardous waste bag and required gloves to administer. The treatment often left Olivia in tears because of its pain and side effects. Wednesdays became anxious as she anticipated the following morning.A friend began leaving a small surprise on the family’s doorstep each Thursday. The gesture gave Olivia something to smile about before another hospital day. That kindness inspired the foundation’s care-package programme for the whole family. First called the Unicorn Box programme, the club now provides year-round support to children facing cancer across the United States, with packages for treatment days and special occasions.The foundation helps families manage the costs of childhood cancerEach enrolled child receives a welcome package containing age-appropriate comfort items, activities and encouragement for hospital stays, clinic visits and treatment days. Further packages arrive during the year for birthdays, summer, Halloween, Valentine’s Day and other milestones. The programme also includes support for caregivers, recognising that a child’s cancer diagnosis affects the whole family.The foundation has a separate financial assistance programme for families in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania. It is open to children under 18 who have been diagnosed with cancer. Assistance can help with rent or mortgage payments, utilities, transport, groceries, medical bills, and other essential household costs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A California couple died after spending the night at a seaside mansion; months later, their three children sued the homeowners and a water heater maker, alleging a carbon monoxide leak killed both parents
articles.summary: The deaths of a California farming couple at a coastal property in Cambria have led to a wrongful death lawsuit filed by their three children, who allege
articles.body: The deaths of a California farming couple at a coastal property in Cambria have led to a wrongful death lawsuit filed by their three children, who allege that a faulty water heater and an improperly maintained carbon monoxide detector contributed to the fatal incident. The lawsuit names the homeowners, Ben and Robin Korman, and water heater manufacturer Navien Inc. as defendants. The case was reported by SFGATE, the Santa Barbara Independent and Noozhawk. John Ruskey, 53, and his wife Kristen Ruskey, 49, were found dead at the property on February 8, 2026, after attending a birthday celebration there the previous evening. The couple, who lived in Goleta, had travelled to the coastal community for the gathering and were invited by their hosts to stay overnight. According to the San Luis Obispo County Sheriff’s Office, post-mortem examinations and toxicology tests established that both died from carbon monoxide exposure. Kristen also had ethanol in her system. The deaths were classified as accidental. Investigators found a combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector in the room where the couple had been sleeping, but it was disconnected.The lawsuit, filed on October 26 in San Luis Obispo County Superior Court, alleges that a gas-powered Navien tankless water heater had a defective exhaust venting system. According to the complaint, the vent collapsed, allowing carbon monoxide to escape into an adjoining laundry room before spreading into the guest bedroom where the couple was sleeping. The children’s legal action also raises concerns about the maintenance of the property, alleging that the homeowners failed to ensure that fuel-burning appliances were operating safely and that the carbon monoxide detector was properly connected.What happened during the nightThe lawsuit provides a detailed account of the hours preceding the couple’s deaths. Between 50 and 60 people reportedly attended the birthday gathering, and the water heater allegedly operated repeatedly to meet the household’s increased hot water demand.According to the complaint, each operating cycle released carbon monoxide through the compromised exhaust system. The gas allegedly accumulated in the laundry room and travelled into the adjoining bedroom. At approximately 4:34 am on February 8, Kristen contacted emergency services after becoming concerned about her husband’s condition. She reportedly believed he was experiencing a bad reaction after consuming a chocolate bar containing psychedelic mushrooms.Paramedics responded to the property, but John declined hospital treatment. The couple subsequently returned to their bedroom. Later that morning, guests discovered both of them unresponsive. Attempts to revive them were unsuccessful. The lawsuit alleges that the carbon monoxide leak went undetected because the nearby alarm was disconnected, leaving the couple without an effective warning system.Lawsuit raises questions about water heater safetyThe case also places Navien’s product safety record under scrutiny. According to the Santa Barbara Independent and Courthouse News Service, the lawsuit refers to previous recalls involving the manufacturer’s water heaters and alleges that its products have been associated with at least nine deaths since 2019.The US Consumer Product Safety Commission had previously issued a recall involving approximately 13,000 Navien water heaters in 2011 over concerns that a detached vent collar could allow carbon monoxide to escape. A similar recall was announced in 2018. However, it has not been established whether the specific unit installed at the Cambria property was covered by either recall.The Ruskeys were known in California’s agricultural community for their work in cultivating exotic fruit crops and developing the state’s coffee industry. They founded Good Land Organics, an agricultural enterprise specialising in unusual fruit varieties, and co-founded Frinj Coffee.Their three children, Kasurina, Aiden and Sean, have filed the lawsuit seeking compensation for the financial and emotional consequences of losing both parents. Their legal representatives are pursuing product liability claims against Navien and negligence claims against the homeowners. The allegations have not yet been established in court, and the defendants’ responses to the lawsuit remain pending.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: An Ohio homeowner who had owned his house for more than 20 years was arrested for trespassing after a dispute with two people he had temporarily allowed
articles.body: An Ohio homeowner who had owned his house for more than 20 years was arrested for trespassing after a dispute with two people he had temporarily allowed to stay there. The guests allegedly claimed they lived in the property rather than the homeowner, leading to a police response that ended with his arrest. The criminal charge was eventually dismissed, but the incident has since resulted in a federal lawsuit against the city and two police officers, raising questions about how authorities handled the property dispute.Ohio homeowner end up arrested for trespassing in his own houseThe incident involved Eric Freed, a doctor from Belpre, Ohio, who said he had owned a house on Campbell Drive for more than two decades. According to a report by WTAP published on July 1, 2026, Freed had allowed a woman, Monika Parkinson, and her brother, Pawel, to stay at the property temporarily while renovation work was taking place.The arrangement was informal. Freed maintained that neither sibling paid rent, signed a tenancy agreement or contributed financially towards the property. He also said there was no landlord-tenant relationship between them and that he remained free to visit the house whenever he needed to.However, the situation reportedly deteriorated after disagreements developed between Freed and the siblings. According to the lawsuit details reported by WOUB Public Media on June 26, 2026, Freed alleged that Pawel repeatedly smoked marijuana inside the house despite being asked to stop. The smell reportedly became noticeable enough for other family members to complain.When Freed confronted Pawel about the issue and asked him to leave, the brother allegedly responded that he and Monika lived there, not Freed. The disagreement eventually turned into a dispute over who had the right to enter and occupy the property.What happened before the police arrested FreedThe disagreement did not immediately result in an arrest. According to WOUB, the siblings contacted police twice in the days before the incident to report Freed's presence at the house. Freed said he was unaware of those calls and that no officers had contacted him about the complaints.When deputies arrived following another call, Freed explained that he owned the property and had the right to be there. The officers reportedly treated the disagreement as a civil matter and advised him that he would need to follow the legal eviction process to remove the guests.According to the lawsuit, one deputy explained that Freed needed to provide a three-day notice as the first step towards having Pawel leave the property. Freed subsequently hired an attorney, who prepared the notice to vacate and reportedly confirmed that he had the legal right to enter his own house.WTAP reported that Freed posted the formal notice on the property's door. However, the disagreement continued despite the attempt to resolve the matter through the recommended legal procedure.What led to the June 9 arrestOn June 9, 2025, Freed returned to the house to check on a problem involving a sump pump in the basement. According to WOUB, Monika called Belpre police after he arrived, following earlier advice from officers to contact them whenever he returned to the property. By the time police reached the house, Freed had already left.He returned later that day to inspect the sump pump again and mow the lawn. On entering the property, he discovered that a chain lock had been installed on the front door without his permission. He removed it before entering.WTAP reported that another call was then made to the police. According to the lawsuit, officers entered the house without a warrant. Freed said he informed them that he was the homeowner, showed his driving licence listing the property as his address and offered to let them contact his attorney to verify his ownership.However, he alleged that officers handcuffed him before he could produce the relevant documents or have his lawyer contacted.Freed was arrested and charged with criminal trespass. The charge alleged that he had knowingly entered or remained on premises belonging to Monika Parkinson without permission, according to WOUB.What happened after Freed was taken into custodyThe arrest was followed by several hours in police custody. According to WOUB, Freed was initially held at the Belpre police station for approximately 4 hours before being transported to Washington County Jail for booking.His lawsuit also alleges that officers seized his mobile phone without a warrant. The device was particularly important to him because he used it for his medical practice and patient communications. Freed reportedly said officers repeatedly asked him to provide his phone's access code while he was at the station, but he refused.The phone was eventually returned approximately a week after the arrest, according to WOUB.Freed also faced difficulties getting home after his release. Without his phone, he had no easy way to arrange transportation. The lawsuit states that police dispatch offered to retrieve telephone numbers for him if he provided his phone access code.Instead, Freed began walking towards his house. WOUB reported that he walked approximately 14 miles over four hours before a Washington County sheriff's deputy offered him a lift for the remaining distance. The criminal trespass charge was subsequently dismissed in September 2025, around 3 months after the arrest, according to WTAP.Why is the Ohio homeowner now suing the cityThe dismissal of the criminal charge did not end the matter. In late April 2026, Freed filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the City of Belpre, police officer Gunnar Smith and Sergeant Joe Fields, according to WOUB. The lawsuit alleges that the officers unlawfully deprived him of his freedom by arresting him at a property he owned.WTAP reported that Freed is pursuing claims including false arrest, malicious prosecution and other alleged civil rights violations. He is seeking financial damages as well as changes to police training on how officers handle property disputes. articles.title: Usina parada e equipamentos obsoletos: o que reportagem encontrou em instalações ligadas a Ricardo Magro nos EUA  | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipe percorreu endereços associados ao grupo do empresário no Texas e ouviu ex-funcionários. Em uma usina, atividade foi interrompida após 91 anos; em fazenda de bitcoin, equipamentos eram descritos como antigos e lentos.
articles.summary: Equipe percorreu endereços associados ao grupo do empresário no Texas e ouviu ex-funcionários. Em uma usina, atividade foi interrompida após 91 anos; em fazenda de bitcoin, equipamentos eram descritos como antigos e lentos.
articles.body:
Uma usina praticamente vazia e sem operar, uma fazenda de mineração de bitcoin com equipamentos considerados antigos e lentos e endereços onde várias empresas dividem o mesmo espaço. Foi esse o cenário encontrado nos Estados Unidos durante uma investigação sobre negócios ligados ao grupo do empresário Ricardo Magro.

Apontado pelas investigações como responsável por um esquema bilionário de sonegação no Brasil, Magro mora nos Estados Unidos há 11 anos e possui Green Card. Ele está foragido desde maio.

A reportagem percorreu endereços no Texas e ouviu ex-funcionários para entender como funcionavam as operações ligadas ao grupo no país. Veja no vídeo acima.

Usina sem operar após 91 anos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Uma das instalações visitadas foi uma usina com 91 anos de história. De acordo com relatos reunidos pela reportagem, o local chegou a ter cerca de 50 funcionários. Quando a equipe esteve lá, restavam menos de 15.

Além da redução no número de trabalhadores, a usina não estava funcionando.

Segundo os relatos, era a primeira vez em 91 anos que a instalação deixava de operar. A paralisação ocorreu depois que o local passou para o controle de uma empresa ligada à família de Ricardo Magro.

Ex-funcionários também relataram uma rotina incomum quando o empresário visitava o local.

De acordo com os depoimentos, Magro era chamado internamente de “The Board”, ou “O Conselho”. Trabalhadores afirmaram que teriam sido orientados a não pronunciar o nome do empresário e, durante as visitas, a evitar contato visual com ele.

Um dos relatos descreve a orientação recebida pelos funcionários: eles não deveriam se dirigir diretamente a Magro nem manter contato visual com ele durante as visitas.

Fazenda de Bitcoin. — Foto: Reprodução/Fantástico

Outro negócio ligado ao grupo investigado era uma operação de mineração de criptomoedas.

Segundo os relatos obtidos pela reportagem, porém, a estrutura encontrada levantava dúvidas sobre a capacidade de a atividade gerar os resultados esperados.

Os equipamentos usados na mineração de bitcoin foram descritos por ex-funcionários como antigos, lentos e obsoletos.

Um dos relatos afirma que a atividade não gerava lucro.

A mineração de bitcoin depende de computadores com grande capacidade de processamento, que realizam cálculos para validar transações da criptomoeda. Quanto mais antigos e menos eficientes são os equipamentos, maior pode ser o gasto de energia em relação à capacidade de mineração.

As condições encontradas chamaram a atenção dos investigadores diante das suspeitas sobre a movimentação financeira das empresas ligadas ao grupo.

A reportagem também esteve em Houston, onde um edifício aparece nas investigações como uma espécie de central das empresas ligadas ao esquema atribuído a Magro.

Em uma única sala do endereço funcionavam pelo menos 13 empresas.

Ao perguntar quem era o responsável pelas companhias, a equipe ouviu o nome de Cristiano Beraldo, ex-funcionário da Refit apontado pelo Ministério Público como operador do esquema no exterior.

Beraldo trabalhou na refinaria entre 2015 e 2019 e era considerado os “olhos, braços, mãos e pés” de Magro, segundo a investigação. Depois de um período de rompimento entre os dois, ele teria voltado a atuar para o grupo nos Estados Unidos.

Beraldo deixou o Brasil em 11 de outubro com destino a Houston. Dias depois da tentativa da reportagem de encontrá-lo, ele entrou para a lista de foragidos.

Negócios nos EUA no radar da investigação

Os endereços americanos fazem parte de uma investigação mais ampla sobre o patrimônio e a estrutura empresarial atribuídos ao grupo de Magro.

Segundo o Ministério Público, operadores financeiros criaram ou administraram 192 empresas e 25 fundos de investimento por onde circulava dinheiro arrecadado com as fraudes.

A investigação afirma ainda que recursos eram enviados para fora do Brasil, circulavam por empresas no exterior e depois retornavam ao país apresentados como investimentos feitos por companhias americanas ou instaladas em paraísos fiscais.

Para os investigadores, as operações nos Estados Unidos ajudam a remontar o caminho do dinheiro e a estrutura criada em torno do empresário.

O grupo de empresas ligado a Ricardo Magro acumula mais de R$ 50 bilhões em impostos não pagos, segundo dados da Procuradoria-Geral da Fazenda Nacional citados pelo Fantástico.

Ricardo Magro e outras 18 pessoas foram denunciados pelo Ministério Público. O empresário está foragido desde maio.
