articles.title: Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain
articles.summary: Mohamud’s reforms promise stronger government, but regional resistance and violence threaten the fragile deal of 2012.
articles.body:
Mogadishu, Somalia – A day before Somalia ’s Supreme Court was due to rule on whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had lawfully extended his term by a year, he abruptly dismissed the chief justice presiding over the case.

On November 4, the presidency removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. Five judges proceeded with the case the following day, ruling that constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not apply retrospectively to those already in office. Their mandates, the judges said, had expired.

The government rejected the ruling and immediately swore in a replacement chief justice, setting up a direct confrontation between the president and the country’s highest court over the end of his mandate and the timing of elections.

The standoff marks the latest escalation in a two-year political contest over Mohamud’s proposed constitutional changes.

Intended to address long-standing structural problems that have hindered Somalia’s reconstruction, the changes have instead deepened divisions over the country’s political future, the nature of its federal system and the distribution of power.

Mohamud and his allies believe stronger national institutions, clearer rules and direct elections will help advance Somalia’s decades-long state-building project.

The deadlock has increasingly spilled beyond parliament and political negotiations, with tensions playing out on the ground.

Two federal states have suspended cooperation with Mogadishu, while disputes elsewhere have turned violent. In June, clashes between government forces and militias guarding a former president and prime minister brought part of the capital to a standstill for two days.

Somalia’s effort to rebuild a functioning national government is one of the world’s longest-running state-building efforts, hampered by a decades-long civil war.

After the central government collapsed in 1991, regional administrations emerged around clan alliances, building their own institutions, security forces and revenue streams.

Somaliland was the first to emerge from the ashes of Somalia’s civil war, declaring independence in 1991. Puntland followed in 1998, establishing an autonomous administration. Other regional administrations emerged in subsequent years, eventually forming part of the country’s evolving federal system.

The provisional constitution adopted in 2012 established a federal framework for sharing power between Mogadishu and the regions. However, some of the most contentious questions over the division of powers and control of resources were deferred as national institutions took shape.

Those unresolved questions made governance dependent on constant negotiation. Elections depended on agreements among regional leaders and clan elders, while disputes over power and revenue repeatedly delayed national decisions in the absence of consensus.

“Control of ports and trade routes, and relationships with foreign governments, gave some considerable independence from Mogadishu,” Jethro Norman, a Somalia expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera.

Norman said Mohamud’s overhaul seeks to give Mogadishu greater legal authority over areas that regional administrations have long controlled, although enforcing that authority is another matter.

“What you’re seeing is the federal system crystallising into two camps,” he told Al Jazeera. “You have Villa Somalia presenting the constitution as completing the state: one person, one vote, multi-party politics, democracy, central federal control over foreign relations and national security, and so on.”

Puntland and Jubaland, by contrast, see the changes as an imposition that undermines the original federal bargain.

“Their view is that the 2012 constitution was a bargain between the centre and the regions, and it can’t just be re-written through a parliamentary majority in Mogadishu when the regions have rejected it,” Norman said.

Some federal states retain close commercial and security ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which Mohamud, who has frosty ties with Abu Dhabi , has accused of supporting regional leaders in their disputes with Mogadishu.

In January, Mohamud’s government announced the cancellation of the UAE’s port and security agreements across Somalia. The regional states, however, rejected the decision.

The dispute has added to tensions over the future of the federation. Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni, whose administration is among Somalia’s most autonomous, has even suggested that the country may need to reconsider how it holds together.

“If a solution is not found for the current debate, Somalis must deliberate and decide on another alternative way to live together,” he warned.

The stakes have also grown with international recognition of Somaliland. Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise the breakaway northern region at the end of 2025.

Somali academic Afyare Elmi told Al Jazeera that the government was weakening the fragile consensus underpinning the 2012 settlement by pushing through constitutional changes it could not enforce in states that opposed them.

“This is one of the most dangerous times the Somali political system has faced,” he said. “Somalis are no longer moving in the same direction on the future of the state.”

Mohamud himself helped shape the federal system he is now seeking to overhaul.

During his first presidency, from 2012 to 2017, his government participated in negotiations to establish or consolidate several federal member states. After returning to office in 2022, he oversaw the creation of another state and made completing the constitution and introducing direct elections key priorities.

Yet the boundaries of some federal states remain disputed, reflecting what Elmi, the Somali academic, described as the haphazard way in which the federal system was assembled.

Parliament passed the first constitutional amendments in 2024 and approved the remaining changes in March 2026, bringing a 14-year review process to a close. The overhaul seeks to resolve questions about the division of powers that Somalia’s leaders left unsettled in 2012.

The changes give Mogadishu greater authority over revenue collection and sharing, elections and the conditions under which the federal government can intervene in member states.

They also provide for citizens to elect members of the federal lower house directly through a national electoral commission, although parliament will continue to choose the president.

Though Mohamud helped establish several federal member states during his first presidency, Elmi questioned whether he had ever intended for them to exercise significant autonomy from Mogadishu.

“Hassan Sheikh always wanted a Mogadishu-centred federal state, with no real federal substance,” he said.

Crucially, Mohamud’s political allies have emerged as the main winners in regional elections held under his new rules.

Ali Mohamed Omar, Somalia’s state minister for foreign affairs, told Al Jazeera that the previous system, under which clan elders and delegates selected members of parliament, had left successive governments without the public legitimacy they needed.

Retaining parliament’s power to elect the president, rather than introducing a direct presidential vote, was a compromise intended to secure the support of some opposition groups, Omar said.

Mohamed Ibrahim Moalimuu, a federal lawmaker who supports the overhaul, described the president’s decision to press ahead as “daring”. Successive governments had tried and failed to complete the constitution, he said, while most Somalis had yet to gain the right to elect their national representatives directly.

“Somalia cannot just remain stuck just because the changes made aren’t considered perfect for everyone,” he told Al Jazeera.

For regional presidents and clan elders, however, the changes threaten to diminish their influence over the selection of members of parliament and weaken the political leverage they have built up in negotiations with Mogadishu.

Puntland rejected the first amendments in 2024 and withdrew its cooperation with the federal government. Jubaland followed after a dispute over electoral legislation.

Both have their own security forces and revenue sources, and their leaders argue that agreements reached without their participation cannot be imposed on them.

The consequences have been most pronounced in South West state, where a dispute over President Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen’s re-election in March has escalated into a struggle for control of Baidoa, the regional capital.

Mogadishu rejected the vote and federal troops ousted him. Since then, forces loyal to Laftagareen have seized several strategic towns around the city and clashed with government troops.

Following Laftagareen’s removal, South West held Somalia’s first direct election for a federal state assembly in May, a milestone for Mohamud’s reforms. The newly elected lawmakers chose Mohamud ally Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe as regional president the following month.

Laftagareen, now in exile in Nairobi alongside senior members of his former administration, told Al Jazeera he intended to return to Baidoa and remove Madobe’s government from power.

He said he had repeatedly warned Mohamud against changing the constitution without first building broader consensus among the country’s political elite.

“Separating powers between the centre and the regional governments saved and kept Somalia together, and making these changes is driving the country apart,” he said.

Not all federal states oppose Mohamud’s reforms. His allies now lead four of Somalia’s six states, where recent elections have also strengthened his Justice and Solidarity Party.

But the outcome in Hirshabelle, one of those states, has prompted further resistance in its Hiiraan region, where political leaders and elders say long-standing grievances over political representation have yet to be addressed. Armed fighters have occupied parts of the regional administration’s offices in Beledweyne.

Moalimuu acknowledged that the recent elections “weren’t totally free and fair”, but argued that giving citizens the opportunity to vote was an important first step.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, followed by parliament’s election of the president on May 15. The timetable is based on the new five-year terms, even though the Supreme Court ruled that the extension could not apply to officials already in office.

Mohamed Mahmoud Dirie, a spokesperson for the Somali Future Council, a coalition of politicians including former presidents and prime ministers, said the group had rejected Mohamud’s invitation to talks in November.

“Our request for a guarantor from the international community for whatever is agreed was rejected, which will make it difficult to ensure that the government holds to its side of the bargain,” Dirie said.

The political divisions are deepening as international support for Somalia’s reconstruction comes under growing pressure. The UN political mission, which supported Somalia’s constitutional negotiations, elections and reconciliation efforts, closed in October at the government’s request.

The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which is supporting Somali forces in their fight against al-Shabab, also faces funding shortages and uncertainty over continued UN logistical support for its operations.

Uganda has begun withdrawing its bilateral troops and plans to withdraw its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, while humanitarian aid is also shrinking.

“Somalia is going through multiple difficult transitions,” Mahad Wasuge, executive director of the Mogadishu-based think tank Somali Public Agenda, told Al Jazeera.

Wasuge said these changes could leave Somalia increasingly exposed at a time when “the trust between elites is low”.

articles.title: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us
articles.summary: India will remain predominantly Hindu, though its Muslim population is projected to grow faster, according to a new survey.
articles.body:
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.

A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.

The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.

The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.

Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.

The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.

It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.

The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.

Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.

If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.

Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.

Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.

Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.

"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.

"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.

"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)

The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.

"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.

"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.

Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".

The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.

Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.

There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.

By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.

Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.

But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.

Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.

The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.

The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.

The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.

One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.

In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.

Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.

China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.

By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.

The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.

And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.

Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.

There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.

"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.

India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed

Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.

South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.

Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

articles.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
articles.summary: The Gambia accuses Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown that displaced at least 730,000 Rohingya.
articles.body:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.

The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.

It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.

The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.

Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.

Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.

Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.

The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely . Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

articles.title: Virginia school district shutters after finding 500 staff members weren’t screened for child abuse
articles.summary: A Virginia public school district will be closed through Thanksgiving because it said hundreds of staff members were not screened to see if they had past child abuse or neglect complaints.
articles.body: A Virginia public school district will be closed through Thanksgiving because it said hundreds of staff members were not screened to see if they had past child abuse or neglect complaints. Albemarle County Public Schools, which operates 29 schools and special facilities, announced Wednesday that all schools will be closed from Thursday through Thanksgiving break so as to “not risk the safety of our students.” The district, headquartered in Charlottesville, serves more than 14,000 students and has over 2,800 staff. Acting Superintendent Chandra Hayes said in a statement Wednesday that, during a review of onboarding procedures, it was discovered that new hires were subject to criminal background checks but not checked against the Child Protective Services Central Registry. The registry is maintained by the Virginia Department of Social Services. “Specifically, over the past three years, there were more than 500 people hired by the division who passed their criminal background checks, but their information was never submitted for the Social Services registry review. We investigated the matter and took immediate action,” Hayes said in a statement. She said “the personnel responsible for submissions to Child Protective Services did not consistently follow established processes.” The affected employees work in schools and departments across the district. “I made the decision that we must close all schools until we have this issue resolved,” Hayes said. She said the district shared the findings with the Virginia Department of Education, which agreed that staff who work directly with children must have their Social Services screening complete before working with students again. The Department of Social Services is working to complete the screenings, with those staff prioritized “so that we can reopen schools quickly,” Hayes said. If an employee is the subject of a founded complaint of child abuse or neglect, “we will act immediately to protect students,” Hayes said. The district did check to see whether any staff who weren’t submitted for Social Services review were the subject of an active investigation or faced charges related to abuse, neglect or failure to report and found none were, Hayes said. Jenna Conway, the state superintendent of public instruction, said the district notified the Virginia Department of Education of the issue on Monday. “While we deeply appreciate the self-disclosure, ensuring complete background checks is a requirement of the Code of Virginia, as well as a school division’s moral responsibility to the more than 14,000 students that they serve,” Conway said. She said the department supported the district’s decision to temporarily close schools, and “will continue to hold them accountable to a full, outside investigation into the systemic failures that led to this moment.” Gov. Abigail Spanberger said Wednesday the district’s prior leadership “failed the children and families they serve.” “They failed to follow the law by not conducting legally-required background checks, and they failed to uphold the trust our Commonwealth placed in them,” she said. Spanberger said Conway and the state’s secretary of education are assisting the district’s interim leadership in correcting the situation, including “hiring an outside investigator.” “My administration is committed to the education and safety of every child in Virginia, and we will use every available tool to rectify this failure and ensure accountability,” she said. Schools are expected to reopen Nov. 30.

articles.title: Elbridge Colby chides Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia, drawing German rebuke
articles.summary: Elbridge Colby, U.S. under secretary of defense, criticized Ukraine for its long-range strikes against Russia, drawing rebuke from allies during high-level talks at NATO headquarters on Tuesday. articles.body:
Elbridge Colby, U.S. under secretary of defense, criticized Ukraine for its long-range strikes against Russia , drawing rebuke from allies during high-level talks at NATO headquarters on Tuesday.

Colby said that strikes “have not been effective … nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.” He also added that they “have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve.”

NATO allies, in response, stepped up for Kyiv during the Ukrainian Defence Contact Group meeting. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Colby’s criticism was “quite a stupid thing ” and that the focus should instead be on Russia’s strikes.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he believed the long-range strikes were helpful. “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” he added.

Per The Telegraph , Colby walked out of the meeting without hearing a classified war briefing from Ukraine’s defense minister.

Kyiv has ramped up its long-range attacks on Russia in recent months. On Tuesday, Ukraine struck the Kremlin’s Kerch Bridge, which links Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Domestically-developed drones struck the bridge’s road section, and missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media following the attacks.

The strike demonstrated Ukraine’s diverse homemade weapons after facing munition shortages provided by the U.S. and Europe. Some attacks in recent months have utilized more than 1,000 drones .

articles.title: 'Sand body' discovered during Time Team dig at Sutton Hoo
articles.summary: Time Team and The National Trust are revealing new discoveries in a four-part documentary series.
articles.body:
A mysterious "sand body" has been uncovered during renewed excavations at Sutton Hoo.

The site, near Woodbridge in Suffolk, is renowned for its royal burial ground and ship burials that have transformed historians' understanding of medieval England.

Now, yet more mysteries have been uncovered after the television archaeology series Time Team returned for a special dig in 2025, which has now been chronicled in a four-part documentary season.

These include an Anglo-Saxon grave and evidence of a second burial site beneath it, as well as beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch.

The excavations, which took place over the course of a month, were carried out in Garden Field, a separate cemetery from the site's famous royal and 7th Century ship burial grounds.

Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist with the National Trust, said the latest dig put the focus on normal people and their ancestors and descendants.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," he said.

"Yet these mounds stood in a landscape of significance to the Saxon kings, as well as one familiar to the everyday East Anglians who lived in the villages and farms."

Excavated from the late 1930s onwards, the site, cared for by the National Trust since 1998, has unearthed countless treasures, including the Sutton Hoo helmet.

During the recent excavation, the team uncovered one of the site's sand bodies, made when a long-decomposed body leaves behind a ghost-like shape almost like a fossil.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," added Wainwright.

Another major focus of the investigation has been the Bromeswell Bucket, a rare Byzantine artefact discovered at Sutton Hoo.

Following the recovery of missing fragments during Time Team's first season in 2024, the team returned to investigate its contents and piece together its story.

Dr Helen Geake, Time Team's Anglo-Saxon specialist, said she was "thrilled to finally locate and excavate the burial" but there were "still many questions to answer".

"What date is the bucket? What lay behind the choice of cremation and inhumation on this part of the site?" she said.

"And what is the significance of the inhumation grave with its tantalising hint of another below?"

The findings are being revealed in the four-part seeries which are being aired on YouTube throughout November.

They raise further questions about the size, chronology, and character of the Garden Field cemetery, and how it fits into the wider story of Sutton Hoo.

Tim Taylor MBE, Time Team creator and series producer, said returning for a new series in partnership with the trust made for some "fascinating discoveries".

"As ever with archaeology, the more we uncover, the more questions we find ourselves asking," she said.

"That's exactly what makes it so exciting, and I can't wait for everyone to see what the team has been up to."

articles.title: Could Trump, Putin and Xi end the nuclear age?
articles.summary: Their meeting could revive the dream of nuclear disarmament that Reagan and Gorbachev nearly realised 40 years ago.
articles.body:
Excitement abounds around the possible tripartite meeting in Shenzhen, China, between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump during the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0, while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.

Dmitri Trenin, who directed the Carnegie Moscow Center for many years and is now president of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly: “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting… would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera while explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States.

While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should aim even higher: Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hair’s breadth, arguably one word, of agreeing to eliminate not only all ballistic missiles, as Reagan originally proposed, but all nuclear weapons, as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all”, and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said.

The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for 10 years. The world’s hopes were dashed, and we have not come close since.

Sure, we’re up against obstacles, and the odds are long. Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff , in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russia’s power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until the largest nuclear arsenals are reduced – meanwhile, China has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal.

That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After his party’s midterm defeat, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy – and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said , “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive.”

This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told Maggie Haberman and David Sanger of The New York Times: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem… Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power… And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle, John Trump, with making him aware of this danger.

In 1986, he sought the advice of Bernard Lown, cofounder of International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW), which won the Nobel Peace Prize, on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and that he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour. Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”

On January 23, 2025, Trump told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of – of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearise, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”

Whether Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but the possibility that he is iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be in doubt. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favour of humanity rather than against it.

The same is true of Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you: Yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.”

Shortly before the invasion of Ukraine, the leaders of the US, Russia, China, France, and the United Kingdom jointly declared : “We affirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought… We remain committed to our Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations, including our Article VI obligation to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.”

Sceptics will rightly point out that this was before the invasion of Ukraine and a series of slightly veiled nuclear threats that Putin issued. But it at least offers a glimmer of hope, especially in the context of a security agreement that promises peaceful coexistence for all participants.

In 2017, in a speech at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Xi said clearly, “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humankind, should be completely prohibited and ultimately destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.”

While not disavowing this sentiment, Xi has more recently indicated that China would not participate in arms control discussions until the gap between its arsenal and those of the largest nuclear powers – the United States and Russia – had narrowed. Fine. To most people, that means China increasing the size of its arsenal to the 5,000-plus weapons that both Russia and the United States possess.

We have a different proposal: How about if the US and Russia reduce their arsenals to the 600 or so that China now possesses?

We see this being done in three four-year stages, much as Reagan and Gorbachev envisioned 40 years ago. In the first stage, the US and Russia pare down their arsenals, while China forgoes its expansion. During this trust-building stage, the wars in Iran and Ukraine would need to end quickly, alongside a recommitment to the UN Charter and peaceful development by not just China, Russia, and the US, but all nuclear-armed states.

The second four-year stage would be more complex, as it would involve bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral negotiations among all nine nuclear-armed states to address the specific reasons why each of the states possesses nuclear weapons and find ways to reduce or eliminate those incentives. Intense diplomacy would be required during this period, resulting in all nine nuclear powers joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The TPNW would give all nine states a 10-year timeline to eliminate their arsenals.

However, they could accomplish this in four years, given that the starting point would be arsenals of no more than 600 nuclear warheads. This last four-year stage would involve reductions, verification, and eventual elimination of arsenals. It could be done in plenty of time for the centennial celebration of the United Nations and the centennial commemoration of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The nuclear age should end well before it turns 100.

If Reagan and Gorbachev could come so close 40 years ago, we should not rule out the possibility that Putin, Xi, and Trump could do so today. As John Kennedy said in his great American University commencement address in 1963: “Our problems are man-made – therefore, they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants. No problem of human destiny is beyond human beings. Man’s reason and spirit have often solved the seemingly unsolvable – and we believe they can do it again.”

A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic .

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
articles.summary: Israeli soldiers describe the psychological toll of the genocide in Gaza, yet many express no remorse.
articles.body:
Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.

If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, support is available through international crisis helplines.

“I think our army is the most moral army in the world.”

Itay Sagi, a reservist in the Maglan unit, describes killing Hamas fighters inside Israel after October 7, 2023.

“I didn’t choose to kill people. I had to,” he says.

His grief is for his friends. Sagi wants to go back and fight. He does not mention the Palestinians killed in Gaza.

Boris Shtonda, who served with an Israeli special forces unit, lost a leg when an explosive device detonated inside a building in Gaza in November 2023, killing four of his friends.

“We lost our friends, we lost our families, we lost everything,” he says.

The Israeli soldiers in the film “Gaza Syndrome” speak of nightmares, panic, addiction and Israelis who died by suicide. They speak, too, of wanting to return to fight. In hours of testimony, the Palestinians of Gaza are almost entirely absent.

The overwhelming weight of Israel’s war has fallen on Palestinians in Gaza: their children, homes and hospitals. Israeli forces have killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to Al Jazeera reporting . In September 2025, an independent UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide in Gaza. The soldiers in this film are part of those forces.

Guy Zaken, a military bulldozer driver, told an Israeli parliamentary committee that soldiers had to “run over “‘terrorists’, dead and alive, in the hundreds”. His co-driver, Eliran Mizrahi, spent 186 days in Gaza demolishing homes and died by suicide two days before he was due to return. “He got out of Gaza, but Gaza did not get out of him,” his mother told CNN.

The question is not whether the Israeli soldiers’ psychological injuries are real. It is what psychological injury means when it is joined to denial, impunity and the absence of remorse.

In The Wretched of the Earth, the mid-20th century psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon observed that colonial violence inflicts severe psychiatric trauma on both the colonised and the perpetrators. When soldiers carry out systematic destruction and violence, the psychological toll cannot be separated from the political structure that enables and ignores it.

An Al Jazeera Investigative Unit examination of more than 2,500 Israeli soldiers’ social media accounts documented wanton destruction, abuse of detainees, and the use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.

The scale of the psychological crisis is growing. Nearly 30,000 Israeli soldiers and security personnel wounded since October 7 have entered the Defence Ministry’s rehabilitation system, the ministry said in October.

About 63 percent have psychological injuries, with thousands formally diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress reactions following prolonged combat exposure. The Israeli army says 22 soldiers died by suicide in 2025, one more than in 2024, up from 17 in 2023. An Israeli parliament Research and Information Center report recorded 279 suicide attempts between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 percent of the deaths by suicide in 2024.

Mohanad Mustafa, a scholar of Israeli society, told Al Jazeera Israel faces “a psychological crisis among thousands of soldiers, but no moral crisis”.

He says many soldiers feel no remorse for violations of international law. “This indicates a very significant moral decline in Israeli society.”

Israel’s public culture has helped make that denial possible. Oren Ziv, an Israeli journalist with +972 Magazine, says soldiers he interviewed described “an atmosphere of revenge, that everything is allowed”. They could shoot if they saw movement, he says, or if they were bored, and “nobody will investigate it”.

Daniel Bar-Tal, a political psychologist, says soldiers in Gaza still confront Palestinian suffering “to some extent”, even when they deny it or refuse to see it.

This suppressed awareness, he said, creates a quiet, internal fracture, a psychological burden that deepens precisely because the trauma cannot be fully acknowledged or resolved without confronting the suffering of those they harmed.

Ashira Darwish, a Palestinian trauma therapist and survivor of severe trauma and torture who created Active Meditation to heal from full-body paralysis, believes Israeli soldiers can enter Gaza, shoot children and burn homes only by suppressing their own humanity. She and other trauma experts emphasise that returning reservists undergo a severe psychological transition when re-entering civilian life after engaging in continuous combat.

“Someone who can exterminate an entire people while sitting there laughing will carry a psychological impact.”

Darwish describes reservists returning from Gaza to a hospital, office or school within a week or two. She warns of anger, substance addiction, domestic conflict, and sudden outbursts of violence as untreated combat trauma manifests in everyday interactions. “Where are they supposed to go with everything they have done?”

Israel’s Observatory on Femicide recorded 34 femicides in 2025, a 48 percent rise from 23 in 2024. Firearms were the most common weapon for the first time. Women’s groups warned early in the war that combat trauma and expanded access to guns could heighten the risk of domestic violence. There is no official data proving that returning soldiers caused the rise, and the Observatory found no link between licenced guns and femicide. The warning is about a society saturated with weapons, fear and impunity, not a claim that every soldier becomes violent at home.

In Qusra, a Palestinian village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the film finds the other end of that impunity. Abdul Azim al-Wadi, a former head of the village council, says Israeli settlers killed his brother Ibrahim and nephew Ahmad, shot two of his sons and burned his son’s and daughter’s homes.

“The occupation army is the continuation of the settlers’ attacks,” he says. “They play the role together.”

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.

The same impunity is visible in Gaza. In NAZA, a documentary built on anonymous testimony from Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, sources describe civilian deaths factored into military decisions and targets watched inside their homes. The Israeli army called NAZA a “manipulative depiction of reality”.

In March, Israel dropped charges against five soldiers accused of sexually abusing a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention facility.

A few do not accept the orders to serve in the army. Itamar Greenberg chose military prison over conscription. Iddo Elam said: “I do not want to hold a weapon towards innocent people.”

Their refusal matters because it shows the violence is not inevitable, and neither is the story Israel tells about it.

Bar-Tal offers his country a choice: “Cut the violence or cut the narrative.”

articles.title: Hotel workers' skills put to the test at 36th Annual Housekeeping Olympics in Las Vegas
articles.summary: Hotel workers from across the country gathered in Las Vegas for the 36th annual Housekeeping Olympics, turning everyday duties into a series of fast-paced competitions.
articles.body: Hotel workers put their housekeeping skills to the test earlier this week in Las Vegas at the 36th annual International Sanitary Supply Association (ISSA) Housekeeping Olympics. Ten teams competed Monday at Michelob ULTRA Arena at Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino in eight events that turned routine cleaning duties into fast-paced challenges testing speed, precision and teamwork. The competition is organized by the ISSA, which is a global trade association for the cleaning industry. Michael Patterson, executive director of the Indoor Environmental Healthcare & Hospitality Association, a division of ISSA, said the competition began 36 years ago to recognize housekeeping employees and give them an event of their own. F1 LEGEND RICCARDO PATRESE TALKS ABOUT F1'S FIRST FAILED ATTEMPT AT RACING IN LAS VEGAS: ‘IT WAS A CAR PARK’ "The housekeepers are always the unsung heroes, whether they're in hospitality or whether they're in health care," Patterson said. The contests included a two-minute bed-making challenge, a mop relay, a vacuum cleaner race and a pad toss. A new triathlon-style event combined glass cleaning, a stain section and a paper towel toss. Some of the loudest cheers came during the spirit dance competition. Judges watched as teams danced choreographed performances complete with dazzling costumes and complete sets. Many teams leaned into the themes of their hotels and the glamour of the Las Vegas Strip. Team Luxor took the floor first in mummy costumes inspired by the ancient Egyptian theme of the Luxor Hotel and Casino. The team's choreographer told Fox News she wanted to keep the routine accessible to everyone. "We wanted moves that everybody can do," she said. When the final scores were tallied, a team of South Dakota hotel workers competing for the first time took home the championship. US WARNS AMERICANS IN KEY LOCATIONS TO ‘KEEP A LOW PROFILE’ AHAD OF CROWDED HOLIDAY TRAVEL LIV Hospitality finished first overall, followed by Excalibur Hotel in second place and Mandalay Bay in third, according to the company's announcement. The South Dakota team also won the mop relay and toilet paper toss. The victory capped LIV Hospitality's statewide Road to Vegas Housekeeping Championship Series. The company held regional competitions before hosting a final at The Box Elder Events Center. Top competitors earned spots on the team that traveled to Las Vegas. Rather than representing one hotel, the team brought together employees from multiple properties across South Dakota. They competed against workers from Las Vegas resorts including Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, Luxor and MGM Grand. "We went to Las Vegas proud to represent South Dakota. Coming home as the overall champions makes this incredibly special," Kayti Ratigan, LIV Hospitality's chief of operations, said in the company's announcement. "Our team competed against some of the best hospitality professionals in the industry, and they showed exactly what we already knew: There is tremendous talent, pride and professionalism right here in South Dakota," Ratigan said. For LIV Hospitality team member Adrianna Young Bear, making it to Las Vegas was an achievement in itself. She said she had followed the competition for years before her team finally got the opportunity to participate. "I've been following the housekeeping competition for years. We finally made it here," Young Bear said. "This was a long journey for us to get here, and we finally did." Young Bear said seasonal tourism can make it difficult to recruit and retain hospitality workers in South Dakota. She said the competition gave the group an opportunity to recognize the contributions of those employees. "We are the backbone to every local town across the United States, across the world," Young Bear said. SKYDIVING INJURY LEAVES 24-YEAR-OLD TOURIST STRANDED IN AUSTRALIA ON MEDICAL NO-FLY LIST Over the years, the competition has also attracted attention beyond the hospitality industry. ISSA estimated that the 2025 event generated more than 50 million views and 750,000 social media engagements. In August 2026, the competition made its ESPN8: The Ocho debut at ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex at Walt Disney World Resort as part of the network's celebration of unconventional sports and competitions. A member of the Bellagio team said the event gave employees a chance to celebrate their work with colleagues from other hotels. The team practiced weekly for months, increasing rehearsals in the final weeks before the competition. "It's an amazing experience for everybody to be able to see the hard work all the team members do on a daily basis," the team member said. "It's just for fun here, but they do this every day." articles.title: Middle East conflict triggers biggest disruption ever to global oil trade, IEA warns
articles.summary: The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ⁠ever to global oil and gas trade, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said.
articles.body: The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ⁠ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday. Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that ⁠typically carries about a fifth of global oil and ​liquefied natural ⁠gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports. “In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran ⁠war,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency’s World ​Energy ⁠Outlook 2026. The conflict has resulted in cumulative ‌losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said. The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and ‌proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments ‌and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz. Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. In that case, global oil demand in 2035 ⁠is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency’s Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments’ current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand. Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS. Electrification growing The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, ‌heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout. “Many ​countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, ‌they decided to build energy at home,” Birol ⁠said. Electricity’s share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, ⁠up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels. Alongside data centers, rising demand ‌for cooling is emerging as one ​of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the ‌first time, demand for cooling in buildings has ​exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use.
